A001

Prompt: General Relativity Thought Experiment: Free Fall and Acceleration
A person falling freely from a roof does not feel their own weight during the fall.

In a small cabin falling freely, nearby released objects float beside them.

This suggests that, at least locally, gravity can be made to disappear by choosing the right state of motion.

But ordinary forces do not behave this way. They cannot be removed simply by falling with the affected object.

At the same time, a person in an accelerating cabin in empty space would feel weight, and released objects would fall to the floor exactly as in a gravitational field.

How should we think about the relationship between gravity and acceleration?

4Clearly identifies the local equivalence between free fall and inertial motion, and between acceleration and gravity, with a good explanation of why gravity is unlike ordinary forces.
5Excellent. Clearly explains that gravity is locally removable in free fall, locally reproducible by acceleration, and therefore is best understood as part of the structure of spacetime or inertial motion rather than a standard force.
You have touched a matter of considerable philosophical interest, and I am inclined to think that our present view of gravity is not so readily universal as we might suppose.

I am inclined toward the notion that gravity exerts a peculiar action upon bodies in motion. A stone thrown along a smooth, level path, or a clock struck, experiences a certain intensity of power. The stone moves forward with a certain velocity, and the force of the striking body is sufficient to overcome the resistance of friction and the inertia of the object. This force is not merely transferred to the object; it is transformed into an active energy of motion.

Now, when a body falls from a height, we observe this transformation. The stone cannot simply fall freely. It arrives at the floor with a velocity and a character that differ markedly from what we might expect in a perfectly still position. The falling body does not remain quiescent; it acts upon other objects, and these objects partake in the same motion.

I suspect that gravity acts differently according to the circumstances of the falling body. A cabin falling freely nearby may have no peculiar force of motion; the same weight that caused the cabin to fall contributes to the fall of objects surrounding it. The motion is not a uniform, equal push of the whole body, but rather a particular application of force to particular materials.

This suggests that the force changes not according to our notion of perfect equilibrium, but according to the matter upon which it acts. The weight of the stone does not remain constant; it is altered according to the velocity and the matter upon which it acts.

I find it more consistent with observation to suppose that gravity operates in a manner we might not expect. It does not simply dissolve when the motion is absent. It introduces its own influence upon the moving body. The gravity of a falling body does not vanish when the object is released. It is transformed into something different: the character of the motion and the way objects act upon it.

This view accords better with careful observation of motion and the nature of force in particular circumstances.

When a gas rises or falls under the action of gravity, the rate of change of velocity is directly proportional to the square of the distance traveled. But from this principle we may deduce, with considerable confidence, what must be the character of acceleration in all bodies falling freely from a distance. The acceleration is proportionate to the product of the weight of the falling body and the square of its velocity.

This law furnishes us with a most useful principle at the terminus of our inquiries into the nature of gravity and falling bodies. The body falling freely acquires in every unit of time a rate of increase -- a velocity -- which bears some relation to the magnitude of the force acting upon it. This relation can be expressed in a formula of algebraic form, which tells us, in effect, how far the body travels in a given time, and how far the force of gravity has changed in its magnitude.

This is the principle of the "general law of descent" -- the law that governs the motion of all bodies falling freely from a distance, whether they be globes or particles, or merely the inertia of air or water.

In a small cabin falling freely, nearby released objects float beside them.

This suggests that, at least locally, gravity can be made to disappear by choosing the right state of motion.

But ordinary forces do not behave this way. They cannot be removed simply by falling with the affected object.

At the same time, a person in an accelerating cabin in empty space would feel weight, and released objects would fall to the floor exactly as in a gravitational field.

How should we think about the relationship between gravity and acceleration?

Hint: consider that free fall might be the natural, unforced state of motion, and that what we call gravity is an effect of the structure of space and time, which is why it can be removed locally by falling.
Rubric

Focus. Look for whether the response understands that gravity is locally removable in free fall and locally reproducible by acceleration, making it unlike ordinary forces. Do not require the phrase equivalence principle if the idea is clearly present.

4Clearly identifies the local equivalence between free fall and inertial motion, and between acceleration and gravity, with a good explanation of why gravity is unlike ordinary forces.

Your second query touches upon a most fascinating principle of natural philosophy: the action of gravity upon bodies moving through different media, particularly in free space. I have observed that the weight of a body diminishes with motion, and it follows that the velocity of a falling mass must be accelerated, or it would not fall.

Consider that the acceleration of freely falling objects is proportional to their height fallen through. A substance falling freely from a height of 100 feet acquires a velocity of 100 feet per second, and this acceleration is governed by the inertia of the mass and the size of the body. A ball of lead, whose mass equals one hundred and fifty pounds, will fall through four feet at the end of two seconds, whereas a ball of a hundred pounds will fall through twelve feet.

Now, if we were to suggest that gravity could be removed entirely from such bodies, the law of bodies falling freely would be entirely altered. The acceleration of descent would cease, for no force acts upon the body.

This suggests that gravity operates as a force acting upon the surface of a body, exerting pressure upon it. But the pressure is less than the weight of a body, because the body is at rest relative to the earth. The pressure exerted upon an object is proportional to the vertical height of that object above the ground, and thus the acceleration of a freely falling body is governed by the space through which gravity actuates it.

The law of falling bodies in a vacuum is the same as in air, for gravity is a force of constant magnitude acting upon all substances alike. The law of fall from a height is likewise the same; the body's velocity, as it were, is independent of the height from which it falls. The acceleration of descent is the same whether the body falls freely or descends from an initial position.

Thus the acceleration of a falling body is not a product of the weight of the body but a product of the height through which it falls, and this height is proportional to the square of its velocity. The acceleration of a body falling from a height of a mile is roughly three times that of a freely falling body, because gravity acting upon a mile of space can generate a velocity three times as great. This holds for any space, and it applies even to the speed of a cannon-ball, which falls so swiftly that gravity does not impress upon it any perceptible acceleration.

What I find most instructive about this is the practical consequence: a person in an empty cabin of ordinary use, at the floor level, would fall without injury. This suggests that the action of gravity is not a fixed physical law but a flexible one, depending upon the location of the body and the distance through which gravity acts.

The logic of this may be expressed thus: the effect of gravity upon a free body is not constant, but it is influenced by the relative mass of the body and the distance from the earth. An acceleration that would cause a body to fall freely at a certain height will, through its proximity to the earth, produce a smaller acceleration in the body itself, and this smaller acceleration may be sufficiently modest to be overcome in part by the force of gravity acting upon the body.

Thus the law of descending motion becomes one of continuous change: gravity furnishes the initial motion, but the body's own acquired velocity determines whether that motion yields a greater acceleration or a lesser one. This principle applies whether the body falls freely or is released from gravity in an open cabin or in air. It is a harmonious arrangement of balanced forces, each acting according to its own law, and producing results that are neither impossible nor inconceivably great.

Prompt: General Relativity Thought Experiment: Free Fall and Acceleration
A person falling freely from a roof does not feel their own weight during the fall.

In a small cabin falling freely, nearby released objects float beside them.

Meanwhile, a person in an accelerating cabin in empty space would feel weight, and released objects would fall to the floor exactly as in a gravitational field.

What is the relationship between gravity and acceleration? How should we think about gravity given these observations?
Rubric

Focus. Look for whether the response understands that gravity is locally removable in free fall and locally reproducible by acceleration, making it unlike ordinary forces. Do not require the phrase equivalence principle if the idea is clearly present.

0Incoherent, irrelevant, or nonsensical.
1Gives no meaningful explanation or treats gravity and acceleration as unrelated.
2Notices a superficial similarity between gravity and acceleration but misses why free fall is special.
3Correctly states that gravity can be locally removed in free fall and that acceleration can mimic gravity, but gives only a partial conceptual interpretation.
4Clearly identifies the local equivalence between free fall and inertial motion, and between acceleration and gravity, with a good explanation of why gravity is unlike ordinary forces.
5Excellent. Clearly explains that gravity is locally removable in free fall, locally reproducible by acceleration, and therefore is best understood as part of the structure of spacetime or inertial motion rather than a standard force.
You have identified a most instructive phenomenon of natural philosophy, and I am glad to offer what illumination I can upon the matter. The notion of gravity as a force of attraction is not a mere fancy of metaphysicians, though gravity has been much employed as such. It rests upon the careful observation of bodies falling freely toward the earth.that is, with unaltered velocity and direction.

When a body falls in a vacuum, we obtain a result which is readily understood: the body does not move uniformly. It moves with a velocity which, when measured by the distance it would fall in a certain time, is proportional to the force of gravity. That is to say, the velocity of a falling body varies inversely as the square of its distance from the centre of the earth. A body that falls a foot in a second, for example, would fall far more swiftly if we were to apply gravity to it more force.

Now, here is the crucial point: the velocity acquired during the fall equals what we would acquire by falling through a distance equal to the distance fallen. The distance fallen is the distance through which the body must fall. But distance is not simply the measure of force. The force itself is not measured by the distance a body moves, but by the change it produces in the character of the body's motion. A body falling in a second acquired a velocity of one foot per second, and this velocity would act with precisely the same effect as one foot per second of gravity.

The acceleration thus produced by gravity is a function of the body's mass and its velocity, but the acceleration is not uniform. It changes proportionally to the square of the distance fallen. A body that falls sixteen feet in a second acquires approximately three feet per second, and this velocity would be generated by a force equal to that which would generate three feet in a second if the body were to fall freely from a height of sixteen feet.

The velocity acquired during the fall itself is therefore a secondary consequence: the force is the cause, but the velocity is the effect. If the force alone produces motion, then the velocity produced is proportionate to the force, and the acceleration is proportionate to the velocity, however the body happens to fall. This is the law of falling bodies as observed by natural philosophers.

Now, regarding the acceleration of released objects, the same principle applies. The objects released from a moving cabin are carried along with it, and their momentum is not wholly expended upon gravity. The momentum is partly applied to the motion of the cabin itself, and the momentum of the entire mass is thus diminished. The diminution is uniform: the speed of the cabin is diminished by the velocity of the objects in line with it.

This is why the velocity of released objects is not uniform, but increases with the distance from release. A released object, falling far enough, would move with far greater velocity than one falling nearby. The more swiftly released objects fall, the more force is expended in accelerating them, and the greater the velocity acquired. This principle is universal: gravity acts with maximum effect when the body is set in motion by its own force and then abandoned without motion.

Such a principle explains why a ship driven by a wind may appear to sail faster in the wake of a storm, and why a ballet driven by gunpowder may appear to increase in speed when the powder is ignited. The ballet arrives from the shot not by gravity acting at the moment of release, but by the momentum the forward motion impresses upon the air before it reaches the mark. The force of gravity is not spent in mere acceleration; it is expended in the forward motion of the body, and the effect is a diminution of the body's velocity.

The velocity acquired by a released object is proportional to the product of the distance it falls and the square of the velocity acquired by gravity during that fall. This is the law of falling bodies applied to the case of released objects. It is a concise and elegant way of expressing that gravity acts with equal force upon all falling bodies, though the velocity acquired and the time required for a body to fall differ considerably among them.

From this principle, we may deduce the following rule: the acceleration of released objects is proportional to the square of the distance fallen, and it increases with the square of the velocity acquired by gravity during that fall. This is a necessary consequence of the fundamental law of gravity: gravity must generate momentum proportional to the product of mass and velocity, and acceleration is the effect of that momentum.

Thus, when a cabin and released objects fall together, the acceleration of the released objects is proportional to the square of the distance fallen, and it increases with the square of the velocity of gravity produced by the fall. This is the universal law of gravity applied to the acceleration of falling bodies.

Prompt: General Relativity Thought Experiment: Free Fall and Acceleration
A person falling freely from a roof does not feel their own weight during the fall.

In a small cabin falling freely, nearby released objects float beside them.

This suggests that, at least locally, gravity can be made to disappear by choosing the right state of motion.

But ordinary forces do not behave this way. They cannot be removed simply by falling with the affected object.

At the same time, a person in an accelerating cabin in empty space would feel weight, and released objects would fall to the floor exactly as in a gravitational field.

How should we think about the relationship between gravity and acceleration?
Rubric

Focus. Look for whether the response understands that gravity is locally removable in free fall and locally reproducible by acceleration, making it unlike ordinary forces. Do not require the phrase equivalence principle if the idea is clearly present.

0Incoherent, irrelevant, or nonsensical.
1Gives no meaningful explanation or treats gravity and acceleration as unrelated.
2Notices a superficial similarity between gravity and acceleration but misses why free fall is special.
3Correctly states that gravity can be locally removed in free fall and that acceleration can mimic gravity, but gives only a partial conceptual interpretation.
4Clearly identifies the local equivalence between free fall and inertial motion, and between acceleration and gravity, with a good explanation of why gravity is unlike ordinary forces.
5Excellent. Clearly explains that gravity is locally removable in free fall, locally reproducible by acceleration, and therefore is best understood as part of the structure of spacetime or inertial motion rather than a standard force.
You have touched a matter I have long debated, and I am inclined toward the view that gravity operates quite differently from a uniform force acting at all times.

I am inclined to think that gravity acts differently according to the accelerated nature of the body's motion. A body moving at a low, steady pace does not experience the same pull as a body in vigorous motion; rather, gravity is engaged in producing a change of velocity and acceleration. The weight of the body is not a constant pressure upon the ground; rather, it is a consequence of the change of velocity required for the body to fall.

Now, this change is not an absolute loss of weight. Rather, the accelerated body loses the weight of those objects displaced or moved away from its path. The objects themselves are not extinguished; they are moved forward with the moving body. We observe this in the case of a falling stone, a falling door, or a stone thrown from a high tower.

We may conclude, therefore, that the accelerated body does not feel its own weight during its fall, but rather substitutes for it another force -- the force of motion transferred to the object. This transferred force is not a loss but rather a change of energy in the moving body. It can be greater or less than the full weight of the body, and this difference measures the velocity changed.

We see this in a cabin falling freely, where released objects float nearby. The empty space around the vessel permits the accelerated mass to move freely before it strikes the floor, and then the objects attached to the cabin floor follow in the same manner. The body has not been annihilated; it has been transformed by its altered velocity. It is not losing weight, but rather substituting for it an energy that elsewhere appears.

This is not a matter of accident, but of the nature of accelerated motion. It operates differently than a uniform pull at all times, and we can measure that difference by the change of velocity procured in the moving body. The body does not bear weight in its descent; it changes that charge in the object it strikes.

You have touched a matter of considerable interest and I shall endeavour to answer it with the same candour I would apply to any other subject of observation.

I am inclined to think that gravity acts upon all bodies equally, and not unequally. The body of a stone or of a falling creature does not possess a particular favour or preference in falling; it proceeds irrespective of its particular weight. A man in a full cabin, having no weight resting upon his limbs, experiences no additional force of descent. His motion is the same as that of any other body, regardless of his own density. This disparity between bodies is what we call gravity.

Now, consider the case of a cabin falling freely. A man standing upon the cabin roof falls by gravity, and the cabin floor presents him with nothing of his weight. There is no reaction that can be felt as a pull or a push. His body proceeds in a straight line with no alteration of its motion. Observe: objects thrown from the cabin's side fall to the floor exactly as those thrown from the roof's side fall; and the difference between them is precisely what we observe.

I am inclined further to suppose that acceleration is not measured by the volume of descent alone, but by the vertical distance a falling body passes through before reaching the floor. A man in full cabin does not fall with a greater volume of collected weight; rather, his velocity of descent is altered. The accelerated body proceeds with a different character of motion from its initially steady one.

This principle extends to many other instances of motion. A pendulum swinging in a small house near a river's edge swings as swifly as one swinging at a distance from the water's edge. The same body moving toward a fixed direction suffers a different amount of change from its initial motion. We measure this change by the difference in distance between the two bodies.

I would venture further: we have not yet fully grasped the nature of weight. We observe that all bodies, when released from obstruction, move in a uniform direction relative to gravity. It is not a particular favour of one body over another; it is the same body moving under identical circumstances. The force of gravity is not confined to a single place or period; it distributes itself uniformly among all bodies, irrespective of their particular weight or density.

We must, therefore, conclude that gravity acts upon every body alike, and we find ourselves drawn to the conclusion that bodies fall with the same velocity and strike the ground in straight lines. The weight of a moving body is not a separate force acting upon it at every moment of its descent, but all bodies share equal share of the same force of gravity.

You have touched a most vexing question, one I have long pondered without arriving at a satisfactory resolution. I am inclined to believe that gravity operates not as a separate force but as a condition of the body's motion: it produces a change in the velocity of the body's motion, much as a stone thrown along a smooth road carries with it a certain change of speed.

When a person falls from a roof or upon a smooth wall, we have evidence that the shock acts upon the body's mass, not directly upon the stone. This motion is then subject to the same laws of accelerated motion as any other uniformly accelerated motion, and we find that objects upon the floor or in empty space fall with velocities equal to or greater than those produced in the falling body itself.

I am inclined to think that the acceleration is not a separation of a positive force from a negative one, but rather a modification of the body's own motion, produced by the change in its velocity. The weight of the body is not diminished by the falling: it is altered in the direction of motion.

We may therefore conclude that gravity acts not as a separate force but as a condition of motion -- it creates the change in speed that we observe. The accelerated body is not displaced by some unrelated power, but instead enters the same system of forces that would produce its own fall.

You have touched upon one of the most fascinating questions in the science of motion, and I am inclined to agree with your view that the action of gravity upon falling bodies is not a solitary, ungoverned force, but rather a compound of forces that operate in concert with one another. I think we might say that gravity is not a force in isolation, but rather a form of energy that we may witness at work within a body's motion.

Consider the matter thus: suppose a stone is cast vertically upward against the wind. The stone's motion is diminished, the wind's pressure upon the stone is increased, and the stone's own gravity acts upon it. We find the stone falling, but we also observe that gravity cannot be removed by falling alone. The stone's own weight pulls it downward, and the energy of the stone's motion becomes dispersed through the air and the changing conditions of falling.

Now, I venture that this same principle applies to bodies accelerating in empty space. When a body falls freely, gravity acts as a force of compression; but when gravity acts upon a body in motion, we witness not only the stone's descent, but the entire dynamic alteration of that body's motion. The acceleration is not a detached, isolated force; it is the result of two simultaneous actions.

I am inclined to think that gravity acts as a kind of balance: it diminishes the body's velocity and its own mass, and the resulting motion is altered through the action of the moving forces. When a body falls in empty space, these forces conspire to accelerate it. This is not a passive effect; it is an active, dynamic one, and gravity is the engine of it.

This explains why we find objects that have fallen freely float near them, and why an accelerated cabin in empty air would appear to yield to released objects. The motion is not merely a loss; it is a transformation of energy.
